gaps.note: All 21 networks. The mirrored ledgers unit took its token lists from explorer pages (Blockscout, Routescan), from a pool listing site (GeckoTerminal) and from a hand list on HyperEVM, 9 to 16 tokens per chain and 248 in total. No unit has listed the currencies of initialized pools on any chain in three cycles. The tokens with special behaviour that the review knows (AMPL, stETH, aTokens, USD+, stHYPE, G$, ELO, v4CRCL, qiAVAX, sAVAX) were each found by an odd probe result on a sample. One method would list all of them without knowing the token: compare the change of balanceOf(PoolManager) between two blocks with the Transfer logs that name the PoolManager in between. It has not been run on any chain.

World Chain, Celo, X Layer, Avalanche, Monad, MegaETH, Arc and HyperEVM. These endpoints refuse eth_simulateV1 and debug_traceCall, so the statement that a zero amount transfer from the PoolManager touches no second token rests on the gas of the inner call and on the balance of the token itself. The verifier of the mirrored ledgers unit did not test the wrapped native token on Robinhood Chain, Elysium, Monad and Arc, did not repeat the sweep of the 248 tokens, and its EntryPoint v0.8 probe on Monad was cut off by a rate limit.

Tempo, Arc, HyperEVM, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche. The cycle 2 critic asked for the special address sweeps to be repeated with a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address, so that the PoolManager is an inner frame with another transaction origin. Cycle 3 did this in full for the Arbitrum family only (ten call shapes on 64 to 70 targets). The mirrored ledgers unit used a stub on all chains for four shapes (value with empty calldata, zero value, transfer of 0 and of 1). The hook selectors, unlockCallback and balanceOf under STATICCALL were not sent through a stub on these six chains, and lead L-209 stays open for them.

Base. The B20 token precompile is the one enshrined token whose node source has not been read for balance writes that an account without a role can cause. Cycle 2 did that reading for TIP-20 on Tempo (every balance write listed) and for the USDC implementation on Arc. Lead L-119 has asked for it since cycle 1 and lead L-214 since cycle 2, and the unit that holds Base did not run in cycle 3. The PoolManager on Base held about 5.34 million OUSD in a B20 token when cycle 1 looked.

BNB Smart Chain and Tempo. Jenner and T14 activate on 2026-12-08, fifteen days after this cycle, and neither chain had a unit in cycle 3. The leads L-029, L-124 and L-105 are worded as questions for after activation. The Jenner source is public today: the callvalue unit read core/vm/cas20.go and core/vm/contracts_stateful.go on the master branch of bnb-chain/bsc. The CAS20 questions can be answered from source before the fork, and the current sweeps of the CAS20 range, of 0x70 and of 0xAACC000000000000000000000000000000000000 expire on that date.

Celo. The public endpoint answered web3_clientVersion with reth/v2.2.0-74cc8bb eight times and with Geth/v0.1.0-untagged-c7ed55b8 four times in the verifier's runs. The nested transient unit read only the op-geth fork and the custom gas unit read only celo-kona, and the two texts differ on whether transient storage written by debitGasFees survives into the main call. Three verifier leads of this cycle ask which client produces blocks. Until that is known, each Celo clearance of cycle 3 holds for one of two clients, and the revision 74cc8bb did not resolve in the celo-kona repository.

Robinhood Chain and Elysium. The Arbitrum unit closed the question of the unpublished node build (v3.13.0-rc.9 on two chains, a local build on Elysium) with the argument that the rollup contract pins the consensus-v61 replay binary. That binds the sequencer only if a validator challenges a wrong state. validatorWhitelistDisabled() is false on the Robinhood Chain rollup, and validation on Elysium is limited to listed validators, so the argument rests on parties the review files as operators. The unit was assigned lenses L1 to L4 only, so L5 and L6 had no pass, and lead L-117 about the Robinhood filter list is still open.

MegaETH. The clearance of the KeylessDeploy sandbox rests on two things that were not confirmed: which mega-evm revision mega-reth v2.2.3 pins (the files were read on the main branch), and that every accepted transaction type has exactly one frame at depth zero. The unit saw types 0x7e, 0x0 and 0x2 in one block and states that it did not enumerate the types the node accepts.

Tempo. The verifier found that evm2 at the pinned revision 66687c18 ships committed_copy, a facility for a transaction nested in the running one with committed writes and an empty transient map, and could not search the whole tree for a caller. The JIT path for TSTORE is unread, and the Tempo unit did not run in cycle 3. Two critic reads on https://rpc.mainnet.tempo.xyz (client tempo/v1.19.0-697ea97). First, a creation payload sent with eth_call near block 50,356,289 returned 0 for BALANCE(PoolManager) and for SELFBALANCE while eth_getBalance returns a placeholder, which supports the statement that the native branch is inert. Second, the StorageCredits precompile at 0x1060000000000000000000000000000000000000 answered balanceOf(PoolManager) with 13 at block 50,356,964 and rejected transfer(address,uint256) with UnknownFunctionSelector. https://tips.sh/1060 says this counter rises by one for the account whose storage slot goes from nonzero to zero, inside the transaction, and that creations by any sender consume it at the end of the transaction. The mirrored ledgers unit did not list it, because its probes raised ledgers by value calls and zero amount transfers only. A liquidity removal between sync and settle would give a credit under that address as currency id (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364), which can only become a claim because the precompile has no transfer.

Monad. The self-destruct probe of the callvalue unit left a balance of 0 for a contract that names itself as beneficiary, where 19 endpoints kept the 9 wei and Arc reverted. The unit could not say whether this is a burn rule or an effect of the state override. It is the one opcode result of three cycles that differs without an explanation. The compiled execution path of the Monad client is still unread for TSTORE, and the swap results of the deployed contract on Monad were reproduced for six mined swaps or fewer.

HyperEVM. No unit ran for this chain in cycle 3. The validator binary is closed, so each theme answer for it rests on documentation, on the two public replay clients and on probes of the RPC node. F-020 stays plausible, and the fact that would settle it (lead L-215: must the address named as AQAv2 treasury sign or send anything) was not looked up.

Unichain. The behaviour test that the cycle 2 critic described (lead L-217: a caller contract placed by state override that walks sync, settle with and without value, settleFor, take, clear, mint and burn on the predeploy) was not run. Every Unichain clearance of cycle 3 still assumes that the 24,050 byte predeploy behaves like src/.

All 21 networks. Part of the evidence in the cleared list describes the PoolManagers that are deployed today: sync accepted while locked, ManagerLocked on settle, the mined swaps and Quoter quotes that the libraries verifier reproduced. Those contracts are other bytecode than a build of this checkout. Such results show how each chain executes the deployed contract and say nothing about the custody code of this build. The two tests replay units showed that the source satisfies every test and comment of the repository. Nobody asked the converse: which guards and accounting statements in src/PoolManager.sol:104-114 and 279-378, src/types/Currency.sol:40-96 and src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57 are exercised by no test. The repository's tests run on a plain EVM with ordinary tokens and one model of a native face (src/test/NativeERC20.sol), so behaviour that only matters on another network is the part they are least likely to pin.

Critic check of assumption A1 on 2026-11-23, read only. The probes of cycles 1 to 3 wrote and read transient slots inside one contract and its delegate, with slot numbers 1 and 2. None checked that transient storage is scoped by address, or that slot indexes with an odd first byte are kept apart (Avalanche rewrites the first byte of persistent slot indexes, F-040). I sent one 529 byte creation payload with eth_call and no to address to the 21 endpoints of state/networks.json. It writes 0xaa to the three slot constants of src/libraries/Lock.sol:8, src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:9-10 and src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:13, lets a second contract read the same slots, and reads each slot again with the lowest bit of its first byte flipped. All 21 endpoints returned the same nine words: the second contract read zero (it returns the value plus one, and returned 1), the flipped index read zero, and the writer read 0xaa. I also recomputed the four slot constants from the strings in their comments with a local Keccak, and they match. The result describes the RPC node of each network.

Seven open leads need a compiler: L-016, L-024, L-028, L-151, L-152 and the two build leads written by the tests replay units in cycle 3, one of them marked high (does a build reproduce the creation code hash and the 24,009 byte size recorded in snapshots/PoolManagerTest.json). forge and solc are not installed and the rules forbid installing them, and L-151 came back inconclusive for that reason. These leads cannot be answered by any unit in this environment. They should be parked or handed to the owner, so that the planner stops spending slots on them.

Celo, Arc, Polygon, OP Mainnet and Zora, the chains where an ERC-20 address reports the native balance of the PoolManager. Cycle 3 walked the core paths across the two ids again and found no gain. The leads about the deployed periphery are unanswered after two cycles: L-019 (is sync called before every payment), L-086 (the Celo PositionManager returns the CELO token from WETH9()), L-104, L-199 and L-218. Ordinary users reach the PoolManager through those contracts, and a router that treats the native face as a wrapped token, or settles native value without sync(address(0)), meets the revert at src/PoolManager.sol:356 or the stale sync of F-014.

Robinhood Chain, Elysium and X Layer. The samples of this cycle show that one hook serves a third of recent pools on Robinhood Chain (0x4e3468951d49f2eea976ed0d6e75ffcb44a9a544), four fifths on Elysium (0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec), and that seven hooks serve the 110 listed pools on X Layer. The units asked who owns these hooks. No unit asked what an ordinary account can make the PoolManager say to them: initialize accepts any PoolKey that names the hook (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142), and every later hook call carries caller-chosen currencies and hookData (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:178-335). The hook is not an indexed field of Initialize, so the pools of one hook cannot be listed with a topic filter, and the counts are samples.

titles: The GoodDollar owner has blocked the PoolManager address on Celo, so 550 million G$ held for pools cannot leave
The GoodDollar token owner has blocked the Celo PoolManager address, which freezes 550 million G$ and every pool that uses G$
duplicates.note: One event reported by two units (the custom gas unit and the mirrored ledgers unit), both confirmed at high with actor issuer. The texts disagree on one point. The mirrored ledgers finding says a sync and settle window can never show an increase. The verified token source says a blocked account can still be credited by agreements, and the custom gas unit says the same. Keep one finding, with the correction of the verifier, and one lead about a Superfluid credit to the blocked address in place of the two that were written.

titles: Issuers of the tokens that make up most pool value on Celo and X Layer can pause, block, burn or upgrade the PoolManager's balance
One issuer blocklist entry on the PoolManager address freezes or wipes a stablecoin for every pool
Blacklist and freeze roles on the pooled stablecoins can stop every pool that holds them, because one address holds all balances
duplicates.note: The issuer control hazard of F-011 and F-028, now reported for Celo and X Layer. The cycle 2 critic asked for one finding with a token table per chain, and the verifier of this cycle repeats the request. The G$ item is the first case where the hazard has happened and should be linked from the table and kept as its own entry.

titles: Two pooled tokens make their transfer rules depend on the PoolManager address: ELO on Elysium needs a budget set by its hook, and v4CRCL on X Layer pays out only to permitted recipients
Cleared: Permissioned wrapper tokens on X Layer (v4MSTR, v4CRCL and the like), whose whole supply sits in the PoolManager
Lead: which contracts are allowedWrappers of the permissioned wrapper tokens on X Layer
duplicates.note: Contradiction in filing. The same wrapper tokens on X Layer are a low finding in the mirrored ledgers unit and a cleared item in the custom gas unit. The facts agree: a transfer from the PoolManager to a recipient outside the allow list reverts, and a take to the wrapper itself burns the caller's credit. Record the tokens once. ELO on Elysium is a different mechanism (a budget in transient storage set by one hook) and the verifier corrected the finding: ELO can neither enter nor leave the PoolManager without that budget.

titles: A zero amount transfer of qiAVAX from the Avalanche PoolManager runs Benqi reward accounting for it, and anyone can ask Benqi to pay the accrued QI to the PoolManager
Any account can book a balance increase it triggers at the PoolManager as its own payment, and EIP-7702 removes the origin check that guards Ampleforth's public rebase
Lead: does the PoolManager on these chains hold market tokens of lending protocols whose reward claim names the holder
duplicates.note: The qiAVAX entry was filed under the id of the Ethereum finding F-041 and is the same mechanism with another trigger: a public call pays a third party's reward to the PoolManager, and the caller books it between sync and settle. The verifier showed that the zero amount transfer is not needed, because claimReward updates the index itself. Record it as the Avalanche variant of F-041 at low, and fold lead L-163 and the new lead about Venus and Moonwell into lead L-207, which asks the same for every distributor.

titles: Cleared: Celo. The fee currency calls debitGasFees and creditGasFees that the node makes around a CIP-64 transaction (nested transient unit)
Cleared: Leads L-153 and L-202 for Celo: does the fee currency debit or credit run code under a transient storage map separate from the caller's (custom gas unit)
duplicates.note: Contradiction between units on a chain fact. The first item says nothing clears transient storage between the debit, the main call and the credit (op-geth fork, core/state_transition.go). The second says the handler clears it after the debit and after the credit (celo-kona, handler.rs and core_contracts.rs). Both verifiers traced this to two clients behind one endpoint. The conclusion for the PoolManager is the same in both, because its lock is closed and its deltas are zero outside unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:112-113). The fact itself is open, and three leads of this cycle ask the same question about the block producing client.

titles: Four interface comments and two test helper remarks disagree with the source, and none of them changes who can move funds
Two more places where the repository's tests and test doubles disagree with the library source, and neither changes who can move funds
Source disagrees with two interface comments and two test conditions, and none of the four changes who can move funds
duplicates.note: Both new entries extend F-006 and one of them carries the ref new. Merge them into F-006 as a list of twelve mismatches. The fourth item of the first entry (take of a currency without code succeeds and moves nothing) is assumption A4 and is already in the state.

leads.question: For every currency of an initialized pool whose balance at the PoolManager is above dust, does balanceOf(PoolManager) at block B2 minus balanceOf(PoolManager) at block B1 equal the Transfer logs to the PoolManager minus the Transfer logs from it between the two blocks? Take the currencies from the Initialize logs or from the explorer's token page of the PoolManager, use a window of at least one day where the endpoint serves old state, and list each token that shows a difference together with the call that caused it and who may make that call.
leads.why: sync and settle credit the settler with any rise of balanceOf(PoolManager) (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364), and take pays out a balance that pool accounting never reads again (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). A balance that moves without a matching Transfer log is either a gain that any account can book, as in F-041, or a shortfall for the last liquidity providers, as in F-012. Three cycles sampled 9 to 16 tokens per chain and found such tokens by chance. This check needs no knowledge of the token and covers rebases, reward pushes, fees on transfer, share accounting, system credits and enshrined tokens with one method. A token with a public trigger and a large pooled balance would be an unprivileged loss.

leads.question: Take the hooks 0x4e3468951d49f2eea976ed0d6e75ffcb44a9a544 and 0x2c668601193e4a081dd82604785e436aff6a2acc on Robinhood Chain, 0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec on Elysium and the proxy hook 0x630e9cac0fff557bd3a01daa111ed253c771bcc0 on X Layer. When an ordinary account calls initialize with a PoolKey that names one of them and two currencies of its own, does the call succeed in eth_call? In the hook's code, do the swap, liquidity and donate callbacks compare the pool id or the currencies with a list of the hook's own pools before they write storage, return deltas, or take, settle or mint for the hook?
leads.why: initialize accepts any address with valid flag bits and records nothing about who may use it (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127). Each later hook call comes from the PoolManager with a PoolKey and hookData chosen by the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:178-335), and a hook delta is booked to the hook address (src/PoolManager.sol:181, 224). A hook that trusts msg.sender alone can be driven through a pool of worthless tokens, and what it holds or decides for its real pools is then within reach of any account. The victims use a hook the attacker did not write, so the actor would be unprivileged. Earlier sweeps aimed the hook call shape at system addresses only. On Elysium four of five sampled pools use one hook.

leads.question: Which pooled tokens on these chains limit what one address may send or hold over a period: a transfer volume per day or per block, a count of transfers, a cooldown, a maximum balance per holder or an issuer velocity rule? Check the stock tokens and USDG, the Securitize wrappers and multiplier tokens on X Layer, the wrapped stock tokens on Monad and Ink, SPCXB, the B20 and TIP-403 policies, and wBRL and wARS. For each one that does, does a take of the PoolManager's balance that is paid back in the same unlock count against the limit of the PoolManager address?
leads.why: take sends any amount the PoolManager holds before anything is paid in, and the borrower can return it in the same transaction at no cost (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 104-114). All pools of a token share one sender address. If a token counts outgoing volume or transfers per sender, any account can use up the allowance of the PoolManager in every period, and each later take of that token reverts (src/types/Currency.sol:82-86). That would freeze withdrawals from every pool of the token without any issuer action. Earlier work looked at zero amount transfers (lead L-208) and at one USDG setting on Robinhood Chain. No unit combined a per sender limit with the free loan.

leads.question: For each guard and each accounting statement in the custody path (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114 and 279-378, src/types/Currency.sol:40-96, src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57, src/ERC6909.sol:25-48, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-175 and the four transient slot libraries), which test in test/ would fail if the line were removed, inverted or moved to the other branch? List the lines that no test and no NatSpec sentence pins. For each of them, name the network feature that decides whether the unpinned behaviour is safe: a native face, an enshrined token, a currency without code or at a precompile, a batch or bundle transaction.
leads.why: Cycle 3 showed that the source satisfies every test and comment. It did not show which behaviour the tests never exercise. The tests run on a plain EVM with ordinary tokens and one model of a native face (src/test/NativeERC20.sol), so a weakness that needs a network feature to matter would sit where no test looks. Two such places are known and were judged harmless: the success of a transfer to a currency without code (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74) and the collection of native fees while a native face is synced (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52). A full list tells the network units which lines to aim at. The check uses only files of this repository and needs no compiler.

leads.question: In the Jenner release of bnb-chain/bsc, which is public before activation on 2026-12-08: which entry points of the CAS20 native code and of the other stateful precompiles can an account without a role call, can any of them change the balance of another holder, can transfer return success with empty data or true without lowering the caller's balance by the amount, what does balanceOf return for an address that holds native BNB, and does any of this code call a contract with caller 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe or with a value it takes from no balance?
leads.why: The PoolManager accepts empty return data or true as a successful transfer (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74) and credits native value from msg.value alone (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354). BNB Smart Chain is the one network where a frame from the system address carries value that nobody paid. The leads L-029 and L-124 wait for activation, and the sweep of the CAS20 address range describes addresses that have no code until then. Reading the source now leaves time to act before pools hold CAS20 tokens.

leads.question: Call web3_clientVersion twenty times on each of the 21 endpoints in state/networks.json. Which endpoints answer from more than one client family or version? For each such chain, which client does the block producer run, and which cleared items of cycles 1 to 3 cite a source that belongs to the other client?
leads.why: The Celo endpoint answered from a reth based client eight times and from a Geth build four times, and two clearances of cycle 3 each read one of the two. Every item worded as the endpoint reports X assumes one client. A probe through eth_call describes whichever node answered, and a source reading describes whichever repository the unit picked. The OP Mainnet endpoint reports a development build and the Polygon endpoint a private patch, so the same doubt may apply there.

leads.question: Settle F-024 with one observation. Read crates/builder/src/flashblocks/context.rs and crates/rcs-filter/src/config.rs of okx/xlayer-reth for what the per transaction observation limits count (the default is 10,000 native transfers, 10,000 event bindings and 10,000 call frame observations). Then look for an X Layer transaction mined after 10 November 2026 that exceeds one of those limits. Does one exist?
leads.why: With the filter enabled the builder denies every transaction whose capture exceeds a limit, and denies every transaction of a block that has no pinned rule snapshot. One mined transaction above a limit would show that the filter is off on the sequencer. The absence of such a transaction over two weeks would be weak evidence that it is on. F-024 has been plausible for three cycles on this one fact, and L-187 came back inconclusive. If the limits count only events that match a rule, say so and close this route.

leads.question: On Tempo, walk sync, a liquidity removal and settle with the StorageCredits precompile 0x1060000000000000000000000000000000000000 as currency: by how much does balanceOf(PoolManager) rise for one removed position, and does the settle credit equal the number of cleared slots? Can the credit leave in any form other than an ERC-6909 claim? Separately, what does an add of one new position cost in gas when the PoolManager's credit balance is zero and when it is not, and can an account keep that balance at zero by creating single slot entries such as setOperator approvals?
leads.why: The precompile answers balanceOf(PoolManager) with a counter (13 at block 50,356,964) that rises inside a transaction whenever a PoolManager slot is cleared, by the text of TIP-1060. That is a ledger which actions at the PoolManager raise, the shape lead L-166 asked about, and the theme unit did not list it. The precompile rejects transfer, so the expected result is a credit that can only be minted as a claim (src/PoolManager.sol:322-329), like the EntryPoint case. The credits belong to the PoolManager account and are spent by whoever creates PoolManager storage next, which moves the 245,000 gas per slot between users (assumption A9). The answer also shows whether a later Tempo release that makes credits transferable would turn the counter into a currency.

leads.question: On Base, Zora, Unichain, Ethereum, Arbitrum One and BNB Smart Chain, which five hook addresses appear most often in the Initialize logs of the PoolManager over the last 500,000 blocks (the hook is the third data word of the log), what are their flag bits, and which of them have the return delta flags that let a hook take from the caller's delta?
leads.why: Cycle 3 made this count for Robinhood Chain, Elysium and X Layer and found that one hook serves a large share of pools. The same count is missing for the chains with the most pools. It feeds the check of what a hook does when the PoolManager calls it for a pool it did not create (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:178-335), and it sizes F-004 per chain.

leads.question: Is there an unredeemed retryable ticket on Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain or Elysium, a failed message recorded in L2CrossDomainMessenger on OP Mainnet or Base, or a failed state sync on Polygon whose execution would transfer or mint a token, or send native value, to the PoolManager address of that chain?
leads.why: Anyone can redeem a retryable ticket or replay a failed message. If one of them pays the PoolManager, any account can trigger the payment between sync and settle and book it as its own (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364), which is the mechanism of F-041 with a bridge as the source. The amount would be a third party's misdirected deposit, so the expected size is small.

leads.question: Through the HyperEVM Quoter 0x108Bfe38532C98f8Cd8D7Ab49c9dDAa3675a1c5e, what gas does a swap use per empty bitmap word and per initialized tick crossed in a pool with tick spacing 1, and how many of each fit in a block of 3,000,000 gas?
leads.why: F-039 has evidence marked inferred from repository snapshots. The Arbitrum unit measured 6,837,251 gas for a sweep over 2,677 bitmap words on Arbitrum One, about 2,550 gas per word, with the same Quoter method. One measurement on HyperEVM replaces the inferred figure and bounds how cheaply an account can place dust ticks that push another user's swap past a small block (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-430).

leads.question: What do the functions of ReservesLens at 0x0000001b173C3bbF3984D417d8614E3eed34865B do (14,142 bytes on Ethereum, with the selectors 0x50183386, 0x5333569f, 0x6df8f9b8, 0x8fe532cc, 0x9169ac83, 0xe4811f2e and 0xf95138f2)? Does any of them call sync, unlock, take or settle on the PoolManager, hold token approvals, or expose a callback that another account can reach?
leads.why: The deployments page lists this contract at one address on all 21 networks, and it is the one listed contract that no unit has read. A lens that calls sync changes the synced currency for the rest of the transaction (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288), and a lens that opens an unlock is one more caller of the custody functions. The expected result is a read only helper.

leads.question: What are the verified sources, or failing that the decompiled dispatch tables, of ELO on Elysium and of the wrapper tokens v4MSTR and v4CRCL on X Layer? For ELO: in which slot does the transfer budget live, who besides the address returned by hook() can write it, and is it cleared at the end of the hook call or only at the end of the transaction? For the wrappers: who can change allowedWrappers and the recipient allow list?
leads.why: The finding on these tokens rests on selector names from a public signature database and on read only calls. ELO keeps its budget in transient storage, so a budget left open after the hook returns could be used by any later caller in the same transaction, for example in a bundle, to move ELO into or out of the PoolManager (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). This settles the open part of the finding and decides whether its actor stays pool-creator.
